Hmm, curious!
Across human history, almost every
society has shared one rule:
you do not eat other people.
We usually treat it as a moral line.
But what if that rule is not
only about morality?
Some scientists argue that biology
may have helped write it long before
any law did.
Today, we follow the evidence,
from a mysterious disease in the
mountains of Papua New Guinea to
a protein that refuses to die,
and to the calories inside a human body.
Our story begins in the 1950s,
in the eastern highlands of Papua New Guinea.
Steep ridges, thick forest,
and scattered villages.
The Fore people lived here,
largely cut off from the outside world.
In 1951, an Australian officer
named Arthur Carey wrote down a
name for a strange local illness: kuru.
When Australian patrol officers
and, later, doctors arrived,
they heard about a sickness that
kept taking lives.
People began to tremble.
They lost their balance.
Slowly, they lost control of their own bodies.
At its peak, around 1957,
roughly 200 people were dying of
it every year.
The Fore called the disease kuru,
from a word that means to shake or tremble.
Outsiders gave it a darker name:
the laughing death, because some
patients burst into sudden,
uncontrolled laughter.
The illness moved through three stages.
First, a person could still walk,
but unsteadily.
Then they could no longer walk at all.
In the final stage,
they could not sit up,
speak, or swallow.
On average, the whole course lasted
about a year.
Over the decades, kuru killed roughly
2,700 people.
Look at how unevenly it struck.
At its peak, about 200 people died
of kuru each year.
In total, roughly 2,700 lost their lives.
And at the height of the epidemic,
kuru was eight to nine times more
common among women and children
than among men.
In 1957, the physician Vincent
Zigas and the American researcher
Carleton Gajdusek published the
first detailed medical study of kuru.
They were baffled.
Kuru did not behave like flu,
cholera, or malaria.
Patients had no fever.
There was no sign of the usual inflammation.
At first, the doctors even suspected
a genetic cause, because the disease
ran in families.
But why did it strike women and
children so much more than men?
What was stalking this community?
The answer was hiding in how the
Fore mourned their dead.
When a relative died,
the family did not simply bury the body.
Instead, relatives ate it,
as an act of grief,
love, and respect.
Anthropologists call this mortuary
cannibalism.
To an outsider, it sounds shocking.
But for the Fore,
it was a way of caring for
the dead and keeping them close.
Some researchers think the epidemic
may have started around 1900 with
a single person who developed a
rare prion disease on their own,
which the funeral custom then spread.
In the 1960s, anthropologists who
studied these customs proposed
that this ritual was spreading the disease.
The body was shared according to
custom, and that detail turned
out to be crucial.
Men usually ate the muscle.
Women and young children usually
ate the brain and other organs.
And the brain is exactly where
the infectious agent was most concentrated.
That explained the strange pattern.
The people who ate the brain were
the people who fell ill.
A ritual of love had quietly become
a path for a deadly infection,
passed from the dead to the living,
generation after generation.
When pathologists examined the
brains of kuru victims under the
microscope, they found something striking.
The tissue was full of tiny holes,
like a sponge.
Nerve cells had died and left empty
spaces behind.
Clumps of abnormal protein,
later called kuru plaques,
were scattered through the brain.
The damage was often heavy in the
cerebellum, the part of the brain
that coordinates balance and movement,
which fits the shaking and stumbling
that patients showed.
This pattern gives the whole family
of these diseases its name:
transmissible spongiform encephalopathy.
In plain words, a contagious disease
that turns the brain into something
like a sponge.
Was kuru really infectious?
Gajdusek and his colleagues at
the US National Institutes of Health
tested the idea.
They took brain material from kuru
patients and introduced it into chimpanzees.
Then they waited.
The results were published in 1966
in the journal Nature.
One chimpanzee, named Daisy,
developed a kuru-like illness within
about two years.
The disease could pass from one
brain to another.
In 1976, Gajdusek shared the Nobel
Prize in medicine for this work.
But one big question remained.
What exactly was the infectious agent?
For decades, scientists believed
every infection needed genetic
material, DNA or RNA,
to copy itself.
Bacteria have it.
Viruses have it.
Parasites have it.
But this agent broke the rule.
It was unusually hard to destroy
with heat, radiation, and disinfectants
that would wreck any ordinary germ.
In 1982, the neurologist Stanley
Prusiner proposed a radical answer:
an infectious particle made of
protein alone, with no genetic
code at all.
He called it the prion,
short for proteinaceous infectious particle.
In 1997, he received the Nobel
Prize for it.
To understand a prion,
you need to know one thing about proteins.
They only work when they fold into
the right shape.
Your healthy brain makes a normal
prion protein, called PrP-C.
Many cells make it,
especially nerve cells, and scientists
still do not fully understand its normal job.
A misfolded version, called PrP-Sc,
has the same building blocks but
a different, abnormal shape.
And here is the frightening part.
When the misfolded version meets
a normal copy, it can push that
copy into the same wrong shape.
It does not need to divide or reproduce.
It converts.
Like a molecular zombie.
That starts a slow chain reaction
inside the brain.
One misfolded protein converts
another, and those convert more.
The misfolded proteins stick together
into clumps.
The nerve cells around them die.
And the body has no good way
to break these clumps down,
so the damage keeps adding up,
year after year, until the brain
can no longer do its work.
There is no cure.
Once the symptoms of kuru began,
the disease was fatal.
Kuru is not alone.
It belongs to a whole family of
prion diseases.
The most common one in people is
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, which
appears in roughly one person per
million each year, usually with
no known cause.
Some prion diseases run in families,
because of changes in the prion protein gene.
One of them, fatal familial insomnia,
slowly destroys a person's ability to sleep.
Different names, different routes,
but the same basic culprit:
a protein folded the wrong way.
So here is a natural question.
Could you simply cook the meat
until it was safe?
Unfortunately, no.
Ordinary germs like Salmonella
are killed by normal cooking heat.
Prions are in a different league.
They can survive standard hospital
sterilization.
Formalin, the chemical used to
preserve tissue, does not reliably
destroy them.
And in one laboratory study,
some infectivity remained even
after heating to 600 degrees Celsius.
A kitchen fire does not come close.
Your immune system does not help much either.
A prion is made from a protein
your own body already makes,
just folded the wrong way.
So it does not look like a foreign invader.
In these diseases, researchers
see no antibody response,
no fever, and no inflammation of
the usual kind.
The infection can travel quietly
toward the brain without setting
off a single alarm.
Imagine a burglar who looks exactly
like a member of the family.
Nobody thinks to stop him.
Then there is the waiting.
Most infections show themselves within days.
Kuru took far longer.
On average, symptoms appeared ten
to thirteen years after exposure.
In some cases, the silence lasted
more than fifty years.
Someone could have attended a funeral
feast as a child,
lived a healthy life for decades,
married, raised children, and then
fallen ill as an old person.
By the time the first tremor appeared,
the damage inside the brain had
already been done.
If this sounds familiar,
there is a reason.
In the 1980s and 1990s,
the United Kingdom faced a similar
disaster in cattle.
Cows had been fed meat-and-bone
meal that contained the remains
of other cattle.
In other words, an industrial form
of cannibalism.
The result was bovine spongiform
encephalopathy, better known as
mad cow disease.
It was first confirmed in 1986.
In 1988, Britain banned feeding
the remains of cattle and sheep
back to cattle.
But the damage was done.
Later, the disease crossed into
people, as a new illness called
variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
The numbers were enormous.
From 1986 to 2015,
more than 184,000 cattle in the
United Kingdom were diagnosed with
the disease.
About four million cows were killed
to stop it.
And by 2014, 177 people had died
of the human form.
Cows are not the only animals affected.
Sheep have suffered from a prion
disease called scrapie since at least 1732.
Infected sheep compulsively scrape
their wool off against rocks and
fences, which gave the disease its name.
In 1967, a related disease called
chronic wasting disease was identified
in mule deer in Colorado.
It has since been found in deer,
elk, moose, and reindeer,
from North America to Scandinavia.
It has not been confirmed to infect
humans, but scientists are watching
it closely.
Cannibalism is not only a modern
or tribal story.
It is written into the deep past.
At Gran Dolina, a cave in northern
Spain, researchers found bones
about 800,000 years old,
from an early human species called
Homo antecessor.
The bones carry cut marks from
stone tools, mixed in with the
bones of bison and deer.
They belonged to at least eleven
individuals, all children or teenagers,
and the researchers argued that
this was eating for food and possibly
a way of removing rivals.
In Gough's Cave in England,
about 14,700 years ago,
people even shaped human skulls into cups.
The skulls were carefully cleaned
and trimmed, and the researchers
think they may have been used for drinking.
So our ancestors knew this act.
The question is why it never became normal.
Here is one way to test it.
Did people ever eat each other
simply because it was good food?
The archaeologist James Cole,
at the University of Brighton,
decided to count the calories.
His 2017 study, published in Scientific
Reports, used modern body composition
data to estimate how much energy
a human body actually contains,
part by part.
The answer surprised many people.
The numbers are modest.
An adult man holds roughly 126,000
calories in total.
Only about 32,000 of those are
in the muscle, the part that works like meat.
The heart gives about 650 calories,
and the brain and spinal cord about 2,700.
Compare that with other prey.
Deer muscle holds about 163,000
calories, five times more than human muscle.
A woolly rhinoceros offers about
1.26 million, and a woolly mammoth
about 3.6 million.
For hunters, a large animal was
a far better meal than a person.
And hunting people was dangerous.
A deer runs away.
A person plans, makes weapons,
and fights back, often with friends.
A hunt for another human risks
injury, revenge, and war,
all for a small reward in calories.
A group that raids its neighbors
also invites raids in return.
Cole's conclusion was that when
ancient people ate other people,
food alone may not have been the main reason.
Ritual, conflict, or desperation
may have mattered more.
In other words, the menu never made sense.
Biology adds another warning.
Mercury released by burning coal,
for example, settles into lakes
and seas, where tiny organisms
take it up and pass it on.
Some pollutants, such as mercury
and certain long-lasting industrial
chemicals, do not leave the body easily.
As they move up the food chain,
they build up.
Scientists call this biomagnification.
It is why large predatory fish
can carry more mercury than small ones.
Humans eat high on the food chain,
and studies have found such chemicals
stored in human fat and tissue.
How much any one person carries
would vary a great deal.
There is another hidden shield
that protects you whenever you
eat beef, chicken, or fish.
It is called the species barrier.
Many germs that infect animals
struggle to infect people,
because our cells, our receptors,
and our body chemistry are different.
Think of it as a lock that
their keys do not fit.
Crossing that barrier usually takes
a lucky mutation.
Most of the time,
the germs in animal meat are not
built for a human body.
With human tissue, that shield is gone.
Any germ living in another person,
such as the viruses that cause
hepatitis or HIV, is already adapted
to human bodies.
Its keys already fit our locks.
That is why health workers treat
human blood and tissue with such
care, and why donated organs and
blood are screened.
During the 2014 Ebola outbreak
in West Africa, burial customs
that involved touching the bodies
of the dead helped the virus spread.
How dangerous a single exposure
would be depends on the germ.
But the protection that animal
meat gives you simply is not there.
Even our feelings may carry this lesson.
Disgust is not just a social habit.
Researchers such as the late Val
Curtis argued that disgust evolved
to help us avoid infection.
Think of the smell of rotting meat,
and how fast you turn away.
Brain imaging studies connect disgust
to a region called the insula.
Researchers found that this area
becomes active both when people
feel disgust themselves and when
they see disgust on another person's face.
It is a fast,
automatic warning that keeps us
away from things that could make us sick.
Here is a thought experiment,
not a proven history.
Imagine two ancient groups.
In the first, people tolerate eating
their dead.
In the second, people feel strong
disgust at the idea.
Now imagine a prion disease appearing in both.
In the first group,
it spreads at every funeral,
just as kuru did.
In the second, it has no easy path.
Over many generations, the second
group would lose fewer people.
In that case, natural selection
could favor the disgust.
This idea has been explored through
reasoning and models, not through
direct evidence, so it remains
a possibility rather than a fact.
There may be a social side, too.
A group that never sees its members
as food can trust one another more deeply.
People who share hunts,
raise children together, and sit
around the same fire need to feel
safe with each other.
Some researchers suggest that rules
like this helped hold early communities
together.
It is a hypothesis,
and hard to test.
But it shows how a taboo can
protect a group in more than one way.
Some genetic evidence points the same way.
In 2003, researchers studied the
prion protein gene, called PRNP.
At position 129, people carry one
of two versions, called methionine and valine.
Those who carry two different versions,
one from each parent,
are more resistant to prion disease.
The researchers found that the
worldwide pattern of these versions
fits what you would expect if prion
epidemics, possibly kuru-like ones,
struck human populations long ago.
It is a clue,
not a proof.
And in 2009, researchers found
something even more remarkable
among the Fore themselves.
After studying more than 3,000
people, they discovered a new version
of the prion protein gene, called G127V.
It appeared in the region where
kuru had raged, and nowhere else
in the world.
No kuru patients were found carrying it.
In just a few generations,
the epidemic seems to have left
a mark of protection in the survivors.
Evolution, caught in the act.
In Papua New Guinea,
the epidemic ended once the practice stopped.
After the Australian administration
banned it in the 1950s,
the Fore had largely stopped eating
their dead by around 1960.
New infections stopped too.
Researchers kept watching the Fore
for decades, recording every new case.
But because of the long incubation
period, people kept falling ill for decades.
The last known deaths from kuru
came in 2005 and 2009,
half a century after the last funeral feasts.
The laughing death had finally gone quiet.
The lessons reached modern hospitals.
Prion disease has spread through
medicine itself: through growth
hormone extracted from human pituitary
glands, through grafts of human
brain membrane, and even through
electrodes that had been used in
a patient's brain and then cleaned.
Ordinary sterilization may not
inactivate prions.
Australia alone has documented
ten cases of prion disease caught
through health care.
So health agencies recommend destroying
instruments used on high-risk cases,
or combining heat and chemical treatment.
An ancient epidemic helped shape
modern safety rules.
So what does all of this add up to?
Eating people carries real biological
risks: prions that survive cooking
and hide for decades,
germs that need no adaptation,
pollutants concentrated high in
the food chain, and a calorie return
that was never worth the danger.
These facts do not explain every
taboo, and cultures differ.
But they suggest that the rule
against eating people may rest
on far more than morality alone.
Next time you hear about cannibalism
in a legend or a horror film,
remember the quieter horror behind it.
It lives in a protein that folds
the wrong way, in a disease that
waits fifty years, and in a ledger
of calories that never added up.
Long before anyone wrote down the
rule, biology may already have
been enforcing it.
If this investigation made you
curious, please like and subscribe.
That is how Miya's Lab keeps following
the evidence to the next strange question.
Thanks for watching.
